Content:
Suppose the random variable [MATH: X\sim B(n,p)] follows a binomial distribution.

Content:
There are certain situations where working with binomial random variables becomes difficult. For example, when the parameter [MATH: n] is large, computing exact probabilities can become problematic due to the large numbers involved.

Content:
Under certain conditions, we can approximate the discrete random variable [MATH: X] using a continuous normal random variable [MATH: Y,] given by

Content:
[MATH: Y \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2),]

Content:
where [MATH: \mu] and [MATH: \sigma^2] are calculated using the formulas for the mean and variance of the binomial random variable [MATH: X\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: \mu = np, \qquad \sigma^2 = np(1-p)]

Content:
To determine whether a given binomial distribution can be approximated using a normal distribution, we use the following rule of thumb:

Content:
- [MATH: np > 5,] and
- [MATH: n(1-p) > 5.]

Content:
To get a feel for how this works, let's consider a few examples of binomial distributions and their corresponding normal approximations:

Content:
- First, consider the case where [MATH: n=5] and [MATH: p=0.2.] In this case, it's straightforward to show that
[MATH: \mu = {\color{blue}{1}},\qquad \sigma^2 = {\color{red}{0.8}},]
and
[MATH: np = 1 < 5,\qquad n(1-p) = 4 < 5.]
Since [MATH: np < 5,] the normal distribution [MATH: N({\color{blue}{1}},{\color{red}{0.8}})] is not a good approximation to [MATH: B(5, 0.2).]

- Next, we consider the case where [MATH: n=5] and [MATH: p=0.5.] In this case, it's straightforward to show that
[MATH: \mu = {\color{blue}{2.5}},\qquad \sigma^2 = {\color{red}{1.25}},]
and
[MATH: np = n(1-p) = 2.5 < 5.]
Since [MATH: np = n(1-p) < 5,] the normal distribution [MATH: N({\color{blue}{2.5}},{\color{red}{1.25}})] is not a good approximation to [MATH: B(5, 0.5).]

[IMG: /graphics/1507bae644c7c2fe2de1006667ee03bc]
- Finally, we consider the case where [MATH: n=20] and [MATH: p=0.5.] In this case, it's straightforward to show that
[MATH: \mu = {\color{blue}{10}},\qquad \sigma^2 = {\color{red}{5}},]
and
[MATH: np = n(1-p) = 10 > 5.]
Since [MATH: np > 5] and [MATH: n(1-p) > 5,] the normal distribution [MATH: N({\color{blue}{10}},{\color{red}{5}})] is a good approximation to [MATH: B(20, 0.5).]

[IMG: /graphics/007aafc33b4905b45a14b08e9e700d2a]

The fact that we can approximate binomial random variables as normal when [MATH: np > 5] and [MATH: n(1-p) > 5] is a consequence of the so-called central limit theorem (or CLT). We'll discuss this in more detail at the end of the lesson.

we can approximate [MATH: X] as a normal random variable [MATH: Y] with mean [MATH: \mu = np] and variance [MATH: \sigma^2 = np(1-p),] that is,

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

Suppose we have a random variable [MATH: X \sim B(50,0.6).] Let's estimate the value of [MATH: P(X=33)] using the normal approximation.

Content:
Here, we have [MATH: n=50] and [MATH: p = 0.6.] Therefore,
[MATH: np|= 50 ⋅ 0.6; = 30; > 5✓; n(1 − p)|= 50 ⋅ (1 − 0.6); = 20; > 5.✓]
So, we can approximate our binomial random variable [MATH: X] with a normal random variable [MATH: Y] with mean
[MATH: \mu = 50\cdot0.6 = 30]
and variance
[MATH: \sigma^2 = 50\cdot0.6\cdot(1-0.6)=12.]
That is, we can approximate [MATH: X] by

[MATH: Y \sim N(30,12).]

Content:
Now, since [MATH: X] is discrete and [MATH: Y] is continuous, we need to apply a continuity correction. The required continuity correction in this case is

[MATH: P(X = 33) \approx P(32.5 \leq Y \leq 33.5).]

Content:
To compute this probability, we transform to a standard normal random variable by [MATH: z]-scoring:

Content:
[MATH: P(32.5 ≤ Y ≤ 33.5)|= P((32.5 − 30)/(sqrt(12)) ≤ Z ≤ (33.5 − 30)/(sqrt(12))); ≈ P(0.72 ≤ Z ≤ 1.01); = P(Z ≤ 1.01) − P(Z < 0.72); = P(Z ≤ 1.01) − P(Z ≤ 0.72); = Φ(1.01) − Φ(0.72).]

Content:
Using a table of values for the CDF of the standard normal distribution, we find that

Content:
[MATH: \Phi(1.01) = 0.8438, \qquad \Phi(0.72) = 0.7642.]

Content:
So, we have

Content:
[MATH: P(32.5 ≤ Y ≤ 33.5)|= Φ(1.01) − Φ(0.72); = 0.8438 − 0.7642; = 0.0796.]

Therefore,
[MATH: P(X = 33) \approx 0.0796.]

  • [MATH: np > 5,] and

[MATH: Y \sim N(np, np(1-p)).]

[MATH: \mu = np = (150)(0.44) = 66]

and variance

[MATH: \sigma^2 = np(1-p) = (150)(0.44)(1-0.44) = 36.96.]

That is, we can approximate [MATH: X] by [MATH: Y \sim N(66, 36.96).]

[MATH: P(X = 70)\approx 0.051.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose the random variable [MATH: X\sim B(n,p)] follows a binomial distribution.

Content:
There are certain situations where working with binomial random variables becomes difficult. For example, when the parameter [MATH: n] is large, computing exact probabilities can become problematic due to the large numbers involved.

Content:
Under certain conditions, we can approximate the discrete random variable [MATH: X] using a continuous normal random variable [MATH: Y,] given by

Content:
[MATH: Y \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2),]

Content:
where [MATH: \mu] and [MATH: \sigma^2] are calculated using the formulas for the mean and variance of the binomial random variable [MATH: X\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: \mu = np, \qquad \sigma^2 = np(1-p)]

Content:
To determine whether a given binomial distribution can be approximated using a normal distribution, we use the following rule of thumb:

Content:
- [MATH: np > 5,] and
- [MATH: n(1-p) > 5.]

Content:
To get a feel for how this works, let's consider a few examples of binomial distributions and their corresponding normal approximations:

Content:
- First, consider the case where [MATH: n=5] and [MATH: p=0.2.] In this case, it's straightforward to show that
[MATH: \mu = {\color{blue}{1}},\qquad \sigma^2 = {\color{red}{0.8}},]
and
[MATH: np = 1 < 5,\qquad n(1-p) = 4 < 5.]
Since [MATH: np < 5,] the normal distribution [MATH: N({\color{blue}{1}},{\color{red}{0.8}})] is not a good approximation to [MATH: B(5, 0.2).]

The diagram below compares the two distributions. The yellow rectangles correspond to the values of the PMF of [MATH: B(5, 0.2),] and the smooth blue curve is the PDF of the corresponding normal distribution.

[IMG: /graphics/8cfafc32409fd0181c8b2844e067b8d0]
- Next, we consider the case where [MATH: n=5] and [MATH: p=0.5.] In this case, it's straightforward to show that
[MATH: \mu = {\color{blue}{2.5}},\qquad \sigma^2 = {\color{red}{1.25}},]
and
[MATH: np = n(1-p) = 2.5 < 5.]
Since [MATH: np = n(1-p) < 5,] the normal distribution [MATH: N({\color{blue}{2.5}},{\color{red}{1.25}})] is not a good approximation to [MATH: B(5, 0.5).]

[IMG: /graphics/1507bae644c7c2fe2de1006667ee03bc]
- Finally, we consider the case where [MATH: n=20] and [MATH: p=0.5.] In this case, it's straightforward to show that
[MATH: \mu = {\color{blue}{10}},\qquad \sigma^2 = {\color{red}{5}},]
and
[MATH: np = n(1-p) = 10 > 5.]
Since [MATH: np > 5] and [MATH: n(1-p) > 5,] the normal distribution [MATH: N({\color{blue}{10}},{\color{red}{5}})] is a good approximation to [MATH: B(20, 0.5).]

[IMG: /graphics/007aafc33b4905b45a14b08e9e700d2a]

Content:
The fact that we can approximate binomial random variables as normal when [MATH: np > 5] and [MATH: n(1-p) > 5] is a consequence of the so-called central limit theorem (or CLT). We'll discuss this in more detail at the end of the lesson.

Item 2 — Example: Identifying Situations Where a Normal Approximation is Appropriate

Given a binomial random variable [MATH: X \sim B(n,p),] if

- In situation I, we have [MATH: n=3] and [MATH: p=0.55.] Therefore,
[MATH: np|= 3 ⋅ 0.55; = 1.65; ≯5.×]
So, we cannot use the normal approximation of the binomial distribution.

- In situation II, we have [MATH: n=60] and [MATH: p=\dfrac12.] Therefore,
[MATH: np|= 60 ⋅ 0.5; = 30; > 5✓; n(1 − p)|= 60 ⋅ (1 − 0.5); = 30; > 5.✓]
